newsitem.title: USA: Regulators seek new plan for Primergy merger.
newsitem.headline: Regulators seek new plan for Primergy merger.

text.p: Federal energy regulators Wednesday sent Northern States Power Co. and Wisconsin Energy Corp. back to the drawing board to develop a merger plan that would provide more competition in their upper Midwest region.

The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, in rejecting the deal as it was proposed, overruled a finding by an administrative law judge that the utilities' plans for independent power systems would resolve concerns about competition in Wisconsin and upper Michigan.
The commission told the utilities to negotiate ways to mitigate their combined market power in a three-month settlement hearing. The FERC then would evaluate the settlement judge's finding.
"We are resolute that we cannot determine that mergers that increase market power to unacceptable levels are in the public interest," FERC Chairman Elizabeth Moler said.
The $6 billion merger of the upper Midwest utilities into a new holding company called Primergy Corp. would create the nation's 10th-largest utility.
The commission suggested that selling some generating capacity in the concentrated Wisconsin-upper Michigan area could address its concerns about competition.
"We give the parties one more bite at the apple" in a settlement conference "for purposes of exploring ways to remedy the generation market power problem," Commissioner Donald Santa said.
Spokeswomen for both utilities said the commission did not "approve or deny" the merger, but instead gave the companies more time to work out problems.

"We're going to take some time in the next few days to review this, but we're looking at this that FERC didn't either approve or deny our application. It established a settlement procedure for us to resolve the issues related to generation market power," a Wisconsin Energy spokeswoman said.

The commission accepted the utilities' proposal to form an independent systems operator for the Wisconsin-upper Michigan area, but it wanted changes to strengthen the operator. Commissioners also said they expected the companies to participate in any state-wide or regional independent systems operator.
Separately, Wisconsin Energy agreed to buy Eselco Inc., which owns two electric utilities, for $71 million in stock, the companies said Wednesday.
